title: Wisconsin Immigration Arrests
text:
New data on immigration arrests was released recently. I learned about it from an Axios article yesterday highlighting the June increase in non-criminal arrests (non-criminal because “being in the U.S. illegally is a civil, not criminal, violation”). The article led with the following chart:
I was curious whether there had been a proportionate increase in ICE arrests near me in Wisconsin, as opposed to the increase being concentrated in places like California. So I downloaded the data from the Deportation Data Project.1
Import data into Stata
clear all
quietly import excel "C:\Users\tjhuegerich\Downloads\2025-ICLI-00019_2024-ICFO-39357_ERO Admin Arrests_raw.xlsx", sheet("Admin Arrests") cellrange(A7:W265233) firstrow
The raw data is detailed enough to identify individual arrests by date and location.2 But here I just need date, state, and “criminal status.”
Collapse to counts by state and criminal classification
gen date = dofc(ApprehensionDate)
quietly drop if date > mdy(6,26,2025) // limited 6/27 data
encode ApprehensionCriminality, gen(cs_id)
assert !missing(BirthYear)
collapse (count) n=BirthYear, by(date ApprehensionState cs_id)
First I confirmed that I could replicate the Axios chart.
Replicate Axios chart
frame copy default NATIONAL
frame NATIONAL {
    collapse (sum) n, by(date cs_id)
    quietly {
        xtset cs_id date
        tsfill, full
        replace n = 0 if missing(n)
        tssmooth ma n_7trailing_ = n, window(6 1 0)
        reshape wide n_7trailing_ n, i(date) j(cs_id)
    }
    format date %tdMonYY
    label var n_7trailing_1 "At least one conviction"
    label var n_7trailing_2 "At least one charge (no conviction)"
    label var n_7trailing_3 "No criminal charges or convictions"
    tsline n_7trailing_1 n_7trailing_2 n_7trailing_3 if date >= mdy(1,7,2025), ///
        lcolor("#FE9116" "#FEC170" "#102BB6") xtitle("") xlabel(#7) legend(position(12)) ///
        title("ICE arrests by reported criminal status") ///
        subtitle("Daily, Seven-day trailing average")
}





Note: Arrests were counted even if they did not lead to detainment; Multiple arrests of the same individual were counted separately; original chart by Kavya Beheraj/Axios.
Then I zoomed out to allow a comparison between the Biden and Trump administrations, also using a different style of chart to more easily see total immigration arrests.

title: Wisconsin Immigration Arrests
text:
National


Expand and reformat national chart
frame NATIONAL {
    quietly replace date = date - 3 // center moving averages
    gen cumul2_7t = n_7trailing_1 + n_7trailing_2
    gen cumul3_7t = cumul2_7t + n_7trailing_3
    label var n_7trailing_1 "At least one conviction"
    label var cumul2_7t "At least one charge (no conviction)"
    label var cumul3_7t "No criminal charges or convictions"
    format date %tdMonCCYY
    twoway (area cumul3_7t cumul2_7t n_7trailing_1 date if date >= mdy(9,23,2023), ///
            color("#102BB6" "#FEC170" "#FE9116") fintensity(75 75 75) lwidth(none none none)), ///
        xtitle("") legend(ring(0) bplacement(11)) xlabel(#11) ymtick(##5) ///
        title("ICE arrests by reported criminal status") ///
        subtitle("Daily, Seven-day moving average")
}

title: Wisconsin Immigration Arrests
text:
California
The same chart limited to California shows a Trump Administration increase in arrests just as large as the national one, with an even more pronounced increase in June.


Create California chart
frame copy default CALIFORNIA
frame CALIFORNIA {
    quietly keep if ApprehensionState == "CALIFORNIA"
    drop ApprehensionState
    quietly {
        xtset cs_id date
        tsfill, full
        replace n = 0 if missing(n)
        tssmooth ma n_7trailing_ = n, window(6 1 0)
        reshape wide n_7trailing_ n, i(date) j(cs_id)
        replace date = date - 3 // center moving averages
    }
    gen cumul2_7t = n_7trailing_1 + n_7trailing_2
    gen cumul3_7t = cumul2_7t + n_7trailing_3
    label var n_7trailing_1 "At least one conviction"
    label var cumul2_7t "At least one charge (no conviction)"
    label var cumul3_7t "No criminal charges or convictions"
    format date %tdMonCCYY
    twoway (area cumul3_7t cumul2_7t n_7trailing_1 date if date >= mdy(9,23,2023), ///
            color("#102BB6" "#FEC170" "#FE9116") fintensity(75 75 75) lwidth(none none none)), ///
        xtitle("") legend(ring(0) bplacement(11)) xlabel(#11) ymtick(##5) ///
        title("California ICE arrests by reported criminal status") ///
        subtitle("Daily, Seven-day moving average")
}

title: Wisconsin Immigration Arrests
text:
Wisconsin
Finally, I wanted a comparable chart for Wisconsin. Because daily Wisconsin arrests are generally in the single digits, making even a moving average of daily arrests quite choppy, I instead plotted weekly arrests.
For purposes of cross-state comparison, I made the y-axis match the scale of the California chart after adjusting for estimated 2022 unauthorized immigrant populations (and the use of a weekly measure rather than daily).3


Create Wisconsin chart
frame copy default WISCONSIN
frame WISCONSIN {
    quietly {
        keep if ApprehensionState == "WISCONSIN"
        local end_dow = 4 // b/c data ends on 2025-6-26, a Thurs.
        gen week_date = `end_dow' + (date - dow(date)) if dow(date) <= `end_dow' 
        replace week_date = `end_dow' + (date + 7 - dow(date)) if dow(date) > `end_dow'
        collapse (sum) n, by(cs_id week_date)
        xtset cs_id week_date
        tsfill, full
        assert missing(n) if dow(week_date) != `end_dow'
        keep if dow(week_date) == `end_dow'
        replace n = 0 if missing(n)
        reshape wide n, i(week_date) j(cs_id)
        gen cumul2 = n1 + n2
        gen cumul3 = cumul2 + n3
        
        expand 2, gen(week_start) // to enable 'stairstep' chart, visually representing weekly aggregation
        replace week_date = week_date - 6 if week_start
        sort week_date
    }
    label var n1 "At least one conviction"
    label var cumul2 "At least one charge (no conviction)"
    label var cumul3 "No criminal charges or convictions"
    format week_date %tdMonCCYY
    twoway (area cumul3 cumul2 n1 week_date if week_date >= mdy(9,21,2023), ///
            color("#102BB6" "#FEC170" "#FE9116") fintensity(75 75 75) lwidth(none none none)), ///
        xtitle("") legend(ring(0) bplacement(11)) xlabel(#10) ///
        yscale(range(46.7))  ///
        title("Wisconsin ICE arrests by reported criminal status") ///
        subtitle("Weekly")
}









Total Wisconsin arrests had apparently been comparable to pre-2025 rates until the past couple months. And the recent increase is not as dramatic as that experienced by California or the U.S. as a whole. On the other hand, recent arrest rates relative to unauthorized population appear comparable to those in California.
There is a lot more that could be done with this data. Ideally someone would put up some interactive charts so that answering a question like this would be easier. If I become aware of any, I’ll put the link(s) here.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
text:
The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) has become the canonical measure of progress in AI capabilities.1 It stitches together benchmarks of different difficulties, allowing the seamless addition of the new, harder benchmarks required by rapidly advancing capabilities. Its transparent, elegant math has helped make it a trusted measure. When Epoch recently announced that Claude Fable 5.2’s ECI was “above what the pre-Astra trend for reasoning models would have predicted,” the ensuing conversation (rightly) took for granted that the underlying methodology is sound.2
There is, however, one ad hoc aspect of Epoch’s methodology that has seemed to me to detract from its elegance. The underlying math can’t handle benchmark scores of exactly 100% (or 0%), so Epoch “clips” such scores to 99.9% (or 0.1%). Though the arbitrariness of this choice bothered me, I came to understand that the choice of which particular number close to 100% they used had no meaningful effect on the resulting ECI estimates—under the original least-squares methodology, that is.
Epoch’s November 4 shift to a Bayesian methodology,3 however, deliberately made small score differences near 100% (or 0%) matter more than they had under the original methodology.4 The way the original ECI seemed to underweight scores near 100% seemed a genuine shortcoming, but fixing it has introduced an unintended side effect. The inevitably arbitrary choice of which number near 100% to clip perfect scores to now meaningfully impacts certain results of interest.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
section: How 100% scores are clipped moves Fable 5.2’s ECI
text:
How 100% scores are clipped moves Fable 5.2’s ECI
In particular, the choice of clip impacts how far above the prior trend Fable 5.2 lands. Its 4.0 point jump with Epoch’s 0.1% clip would instead be 3.4 points with a 1% clip, or up to 6.8 points with a 10−12 clip, 2 times the 1% clip’s result.5 The jump would be even higher for clips still closer to the actual scores of exactly 100% (or 0%).6
Whether the jump lands outside the trend’s 90% prediction interval also depends on the clip. With Epoch’s 0.1% clip, Fable 5.2 sits just inside the interval’s upper edge, as in Epoch’s chart. With a 0.01% clip or tighter, it lands above the interval. That said, the size of the jump is fairly stable for clips near Epoch’s choice of 0.1%.







                                                


Figure 2: Claude Fable 5.2’s ECI from a full refit using the given clip, minus that fit’s own trend prediction at Fable 5.2’s release date. Each line is one fit’s reasoning-era frontier trend (best reasoning models on release, o1-mini through Claude Fable 5.1, as in Epoch’s chart), with its 90% prediction interval shaded. The extended-support beta (XB, described below) gap rounds to the 1% clip’s.




The reason Fable 5.2’s score shifts relative to others is that it boasts a perfect score on both FrontierMath Tier 4 and FrontierMath Tiers 1–3,7 out of only 10 benchmark scores currently available for Fable 5.2. Smaller clips therefore pull Fable 5.2’s ECI higher relative to models without these perfect scores, as explained further in the following sections.
Using the original least-squares methodology (my refit of Epoch’s earlier code on the same data), however, the impact of different clip values is barely perceptible: Fable 5.2 lands 5.72 ECI points above the trend at a 1% clip, 5.63 at 0.1%, and 5.62 at every clip from 0.01% to 10−12.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
section: The clip choice also shifts Sol v. Astra
text:
The clip choice also shifts Sol v. Astra
GPT-6.1 Sol similarly benefits relative to other models from smaller clips due to its rare perfect score on FrontierMath Tier 4. In the official ECI, GPT-6.1 Sol narrowly trails GPT-6 Astra by 0.29 ECI points, with probability 39% that Sol is actually ahead.8 Moving the clip to 10⁻⁵ is enough to give GPT-6.1 Sol the edge, and clips still closer to the actual scores of 0% and 100% widen its lead.9

The probability that 6.1 Sol is ahead of Astra rises from 0.27 at a 1% clip to 0.79 at 10−12. A tighter clip treats Sol’s perfect score on FrontierMath Tier 4 as ever stronger evidence.




                                                


Figure 3: The probability that GPT-6.1 Sol is ahead of GPT-6 Astra in full refits of Epoch’s model, by clip. The labels give Sol’s lead in ECI points. The diamond shows the extended-support beta result (XB, described below), placed at the clip it resembles at the boundary, δ / (1 + 2δ).




Tighter clips result in a higher ECI for GPT-6.1 Sol than GPT-6 Astra’s even though Astra scores at least as high as 6.1 Sol on every shared benchmark except FrontierMath Tier 4. Figure 4 below illustrates all benchmark scores that go into determining each model’s ECI.10






Figure 4: GPT-6 Astra’s and GPT-6.1 Sol’s scores on each benchmark (as Epoch rescales them; the higher in bold), each placed at the ECI that score implies under Epoch’s current method (the capability at which it would be most likely). Each line runs from 0.1% to 99.9% (so Epoch’s clip assigns a 100% score to its right end), with ticks at 10%, 20%, …, 90%. Dashed lines show the two models’ ECIs.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
section: How the clip impacts ECI estimates
text:
How the clip impacts ECI estimates
What the clip choice directly changes is the placement of a perfect score on the ECI scale. Figure 5 below shows the row for FrontierMath Tier 4 from the benchmark comparison of Astra and Sol above, redrawn for four different clips:11 Astra’s 40/41 implies an ECI around 171 regardless. Sol’s perfect 41/41 has no place on the scale unless it is clipped, so where it lands depends on the clip: 176 with Epoch’s 99.9%, 178 with 99.99%, up to 183 with twelve nines.
Nothing about the models differs between the rows. Sol solved the same 41 problems in each case. What differs is how much better than 40/41 the ECI methodology is told a perfect score is. Under the original least-squares method the answer hardly mattered. Under the new Bayesian method, there is no natural limit to how much it matters: each tightening of the clip pushes the end of the scale further out.




                                                


Figure 5: What a perfect score is worth depends on where it is clipped. Each line is FrontierMath Tier 4’s scale from Figure 4, marked at the ECI each score implies under Epoch’s model. Astra’s dot does not depend on the clip; GPT-6.1 Sol’s 100% sits wherever the clip puts the end of the scale. Hover for details.




A more indirect way the clip affects results is that it raises the estimated scatter σb of benchmarks with 0% (or 100%) scores, reducing their influence overall.12 A benchmark’s influence in determining ECIs falls roughly as 1/σb2. In particular, for Mystery Game Puzzles, with 14 scores of 0%, σb is 0.150 with Epoch’s 0.1% clip, 0.171 with 0.01%, and 0.243 at 10−12.13 So a 0.01% clip would give it about 22% less weight than Epoch’s 0.1% does, whether intended or not.
Still, it is generally true that most ECI results are not sensitive to the clip choice. For instance, models at ECI 150+ move by only 0.06 on average between the 0.1% and 0.01% clips (at most 0.68).

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
section: A small fix: the extended-support beta (XB)
text:
A small fix: the extended-support beta (XB)
Fortunately, a small change to Epoch’s new Bayesian methodology would allow for direct handling of 0% and 100% scores, eliminating the need for a clip. The idea is to extend the beta distribution (used to model the score on a given benchmark, given an ECI and other relevant parameters) to a slightly wider interval, [−δ, 1 + δ], and use the probability mass outside the [0, 1] interval to represent the probability of exact 0% or 100% scores.14 Kosmidis and Zeileis (2026)15 call this the extended-support beta (XB),16 available in R’s betareg since version 3.2-0.
The δ is estimated, not chosen like Epoch’s current clip. For the current ECI data, it is estimated as 0.37% (90% interval 0.25%–0.53%).17
The results are broadly similar to the current official ECI, but models at ECI 150+ do shift by 0.30 points on average, somewhat more than under any of the alternative clips considered above (at most 0.24). The largest change is for Fable 5.2 itself, whose ECI falls from 174.2 to 172.9. But the trend line shifts down as well, so its gap above the trend falls by less (from 4.0 to 3.4). XB’s Astra v. 6.1 Sol result is in between that for the official ECI and a 1% clip, as shown in Figure 3 above.

XB measures of fit
In terms of fit, the extended beta has overall log predictive density (PSIS-LOO) higher by 34.7 (SE 12.1).18 Broken down, it’s +73.6 on 0% and 100% scores, but −38.9 on the rest. So the gain comes entirely from the 0% and 100% scores, whereas the scores in between are predicted somewhat worse.
The other measures below follow Epoch’s report (main text and Appendix B).19

The extended-beta is similar on accuracy and 90% coverage, closer on 99% coverage, and better on coverage near 0% (85.5% against 81.0%), a weak spot Epoch’s report flags. Near 100%, both over-cover, though XB somewhat more, and its 50% coverage is a bit further off (51.7% against 50.9%). The beta-scaled RMSE is a particular weak point for XB.


XB+: median-centered beta with capability-scale noise also
The relative weaknesses in XB’s predictive fit are largely remedied by two further changes (“XB+”), which together add just one parameter: centering the beta on the latent score’s median rather than its mean (so the logistic curve corresponds to the benchmark score a given ECI beats half the time, rather than the mean of the skewed beta distribution) and adding noise to a model’s capability on a given benchmark (explicitly modeling imperfect correlation of benchmarks with the one-dimensional ECI scale).20 The estimated ECI for Fable, 172.9, and its gap above trend, 3.4, are the same as for plain XB.21
The resulting alternative predicts better than XB (log predictive density +21.3, SE 8.9: −13.4 on 0% and 100% scores but +34.7 on scores between 0% and 100%), recovering most of what XB lost to Epoch’s model on intermediate scores, and +56.0 (SE 14.1) over Epoch’s model overall. The beta-scaled RMSE is 0.1103 against 0.1136 for XB (Epoch 0.1094). More broadly, though, the point here is not that XB is the ideal model but rather that at least one reasonable alternative to the ad hoc clip is available.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
text:
Conclusions
In the end, Epoch’s current ECI with a 0.1% clip yields results similar to my proposed extended beta, both in terms of Fable 5.2’s jump above trend and the relative ratings of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. These similar results provide reassurance about the robustness of the current ECI’s results. Alternatively, Epoch could adopt the more conceptually coherent XB approach (or a better alternative addressing XB’s relative weaknesses in terms of predictive fit) and leave behind the need to choose a clip.
Data: Epoch AI Benchmarking Hub (CC BY 4.0), as of November 10, 2026.
AI use: Opus 5.5 developed and ran all code. Fable 5.2 checked it, and I provide it for inspection. Opus 5.5 also, in conversation, suggested the extended beta alternative. The writing is mine.

title: Handling 100% scores in the Bayesian ECI
text:
Footnotes


For example, Ethan Mollick’s “30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)” (October 20) uses the ECI for its two initial charts showing the pace of frontier model progress. Likewise, Anthropic’s internal version of the ECI is central to METR’s recent report on AI R&D acceleration there (November 5).↩︎
Rightly, that is, aside from the lack of tether to a relevant cardinal measure that afflicts all attempts to quantify the rate of AI progress.↩︎
The primary motivation for changing methodologies seems to be the benefits a Bayesian model provides in terms of better grounded error bounds and improved model comparisons, which I agree are alone well worth the change.↩︎
“The previous frequentist methodology, which minimized the squared prediction error, is comparable to a Bayesian model with a normal distribution that has the same noise for every predicted score. When using least-squares minimization, predicting 50% against an observed 55% is penalized just as much as predicting 90% against 95%. However, it seems reasonable to expect the noise to shrink as the predicted score gets close to 0 or 100%.”↩︎
Under the extended-support beta (XB) proposed below, Fable is 3.4 ECI points above trend, also inside the trend’s 90% prediction interval.↩︎
One might think the clip should be as small as possible, since 99.9999% is closer to a true 100% than 99.9% is. But the results do not settle down as the clip shrinks: at 10−12, Fable 5.2’s gap is still growing by about 0.3 points with each tenfold tightening. Alternatively, one could argue for a larger clip proportionate to benchmarks’ resolutions based on their question counts. (FrontierMath Tier 4 has 41 questions.)↩︎
Epoch now considers its score of 95% on the latter the maximum possible.↩︎
These numbers are from my rerun of Epoch’s code (needed to vary the clip). Epoch publishes Astra 169.16 and Sol 168.87.↩︎
Using the original least-squares methodology (my refit of Epoch’s earlier code on the current data), I confirmed that the clip barely matters: 6.1 Sol trails Astra by 0.90 ECI points at a 1% clip, 0.88 at 0.1%, and 0.87 at every clip from 0.01% to 10−12.↩︎
In a future post, I plan to provide a tool for comparing any two models benchmark by benchmark, also showing how much each score affects the models’ ECIs.↩︎
The benchmark’s difficulty and slope are held fixed for illustrative purposes here, though in a full refit they adjust in response to the clip changes.↩︎
A note in Epoch’s code acknowledges this channel, explaining that the clip “is not a free numerical tolerance” because shrinking it “hands the likelihood an unbounded reward” for pushing 0% rows down, “and the model pays for it by lowering the capability of the models involved and raising the sigma of the benchmarks carrying the zeros.” (eci-public, bayesian.py)↩︎
Its σb under XB, described below, is 0.147.↩︎
This approach is conceptually similar to the Censored Normal alternative likelihood Epoch tried, as reported in their post’s Appendix A.↩︎
Kosmidis and Zeileis (2026) Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C 75: 139–157 (open access).↩︎
The model their paper actually recommends, XBX, is a continuous mixture of XB distributions in which the exceedance, δ, follows an exponential distribution with unknown mean ν. They say this shrinks XB towards the beta to avoid certain identifiability problems that do not arise here because δ is small and tightly estimated (and its estimate barely moves under tighter or flatter priors). As a check, I also fit XBX (estimating a mean exceedance ν of 0.50%). It gives broadly similar answers (Fable 5.2’s gap above the trend 3.1 against XB’s 3.4; 6.1 Sol − Astra −0.56 against −0.41) and fits slightly better (log predictive density +5.6, SE 2.5)—but not enough to justify the additional conceptual complexity.↩︎
One implication is that the latent mean now reaches 100% at a finite capability: 48 ECI points above the median benchmark’s 50% point.↩︎
The two models’ likelihoods cannot be compared directly because they treat 0% and 100% scores differently: Epoch’s model assigns the clipped score a probability density, while XB assigns the exact 0% or 100% a probability. So I score both models on the same set of outcomes. A score of 0.1% or below counts as the event “bottom” and one of 99.9% or above as the event “top,” and each model is credited with the probability it gives that event (for Epoch’s model, its fitted beta’s probability below 0.1% or above 99.9%). Every other score is credited with its density. (No observed benchmark score lies strictly between 0% and 0.1% or between 99.9% and 100%.) The measures in the table below apply the same convention to Epoch’s model: a simulated score beyond its clip counts as an exact 0% or 100%.↩︎
Note that the observed share of scores below 0.1%, the target of the final row, is 2.1%.↩︎
Gaussian capability noise with standard deviation τ (in ECI units) effectively provides additional score noise that shrinks toward 0% and 100% faster than the beta’s own—more so on steeper benchmarks. Rather than modeling such noise directly (requiring longer computation time), it is roughly equivalent to modify the variance of the beta as if there were capability noise: the beta’s concentration becomes κ + 1 = 1 / (4σb2 + (αbτ)2μ(1 − μ)), where αb is the benchmark’s slope and μ the logistic curve’s value. (Averaging the likelihood over the capability noise directly gives essentially the same fit, at about 20 times the computing cost.) τ is estimated to be 1.6 ECI points (90% interval 1.2–1.9), and the median σb falls from 0.093 to 0.077. δ is estimated as 0.59% (90% interval 0.43%–0.79%), with the latent median thus reaching 100% at 42 ECI points above the median benchmark’s 50% point.↩︎
The average shift relative to Epoch for models at ECI 150+ is a little larger, however: 0.50 ECI points. And the 6.1 Sol − Astra ECI difference is −0.55, against −0.41 for XB.↩︎

title: Decomposing the Epoch Capabilities Index
text: The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) puts 258 AI models on a single scale. What differences in that number ultimately mean boil down to scores on 57 different benchmarks. Figure 1 below shows, for any pair of frontier or near-frontier models, how benchmark scores determine their ECIs.

title: Decomposing the Epoch Capabilities Index
text:
The math underlying the ECI
Very briefly, an AI model’s score on a given benchmark is modeled as a function of its capability \(C_m\) (also referred as its ECI): \[
y_{mb} = S\big(\alpha_b \, [C_m - D_b]\big)
\tag{1}\]
where \(D_b\) is the benchmark difficulty, \(\alpha_b\) the benchmark slope, and \(S(x) = 1 / (1 + e^{-x})\) is the S-shaped logistic curve rising from 0 to 1. The scatter of the “noise” in each benchmark’s scores is denoted \(\sigma_b\). Epoch fits all the capabilities, difficulties, slopes, and \(\sigma_b\)’s at once as a Bayesian model.

title: Decomposing the Epoch Capabilities Index
section: Interpreting a model’s ECI via its scores
text:
Interpreting a model’s ECI via its scores
Because all parameters are fit jointly, each benchmark score influences the difficulty, slope, and scatter parameters at the same time as it influences a model’s ECI, \(C_m\). As an approximation, though, we can use the estimated values of each benchmark’s difficulty, slope, and \(\sigma_b\) to assess the influence of a given benchmark score on \(C_m\). Each individual benchmark score can then be thought of as a separate measurement of capability: a score \(y_{mb}\) implies \(\hat{C}_{mb}\), the capability at which that score is most likely.1 A model’s ECI can be thought of as a weighted average of these measurements, \(C_m \approx \sum_b w_{mb} \hat{C}_{mb} / \sum_b w_{mb}\), with weights that are, approximately,2
\[
w_{mb} \propto \frac{\alpha_b^2 \, \hat{p}_{mb} (1 - \hat{p}_{mb})}{\sigma_b^2}, \qquad \hat{p}_{mb} = S\big(\alpha_b \, [C_m - D_b]\big)
\tag{2}\]
A benchmark score counts most when the corresponding part of that benchmark’s curve is steep and there is little noise. A score near the top or bottom ends of a benchmark, or one anywhere on a benchmark whose estimated curve is flat, counts for little. Otherwise, the scatter \(\sigma_b\) of benchmark noise runs from 0.040 (METR Time Horizons) to 0.179 (MirrorCode), so, other things equal, a score on the former counts about 20 times as much as one on the latter.
(The chart below can optionally display analogous measures for an alternative ECI fit, XCI v0.1 . It is the XB+ variant with the addition of benchmark-specific capability noise, \(\tau_b\).)






Figure 1: ECIs as weighted averages of benchmarks. Dots are the ECIs individual benchmark scores imply, the bars are the weights, and a dashed line shows each model’s ECI. Hover over or tap a dot for the score behind it.



The effective number of benchmarks behind a score can be summarized as \(1 / \sum_b (\text{share}_{mb})^2\): about 7 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 10 for Claude Opus 5.5, whose top four benchmarks (WeirdML v3, Remote Labor Index, FrontierSWE, EBR-bench) carry 55% of the weight.
Data: Epoch AI Benchmarking Hub (CC BY 4.0), as of November 20, 2026.

title: Decomposing the Epoch Capabilities Index
text:
Footnotes


For mid-range scores this is close to inverting Equation 1, \(D_b + S^{-1}(y_{mb}) / \alpha_b\) with \(S^{-1}(s) = \ln[s / (1 - s)]\). Near 0% or 100% it can differ by a few ECI points, because the assumed noise there is lopsided.↩︎
Equation 2 approximates the information a score carries about \(C_m\) under Epoch’s likelihood, \([\alpha_b \hat{p}_{mb} (1 - \hat{p}_{mb})]^2 \kappa_b^2 [\psi'(\hat{p}_{mb} \kappa_b) + \psi'((1 - \hat{p}_{mb}) \kappa_b)]\) with \(\kappa_b = 1 / (4 \sigma_b^2) - 1\) and \(\psi'\) the trigamma function. The weight shares shown in Figure 1 use these more exact weights, which make the weighted average the capability that best fits the model’s scores given every benchmark’s fitted curve and scatter. Not included in the calculations depicted in Figure 1 is the way Epoch’s ECI also averages over uncertainty in the benchmark curves, so the two differ slightly: by 0.03 points for the median model at ECI 150 and above, and at most 0.17. (Epoch does not publish \(\sigma_b\) updates, so the values here come from a refit of Epoch’s published model code, which reproduces its ECI to within sampling error.)↩︎
